rv.q: The stark, unflinching treatment of this subject matter is well realised on Anna Yates's set, and it does not sugarcoat the emotionally messy nature of the process.
And it really does shine on the Donmar's small stage, where an audience can see close-up how a single space shifts from an impersonal meeting place into an almost spiritual site of reconciliation.
Much of the film's more agonising detail is squandered.

But it’s all irrelevant to the plot, and it feels like either more should have been made of these characters or much less. Four great Brit actors play the parents, and I suppose it’s a very small spoiler to say that at first we’re not entirely sure who is mum and dad to the victim, and who the shooter.
That's the best play I'll see this year.

cn.t: Critics praise this intimate, powerfully performed drama about parents confronting tragedy, with strong marks for its thoughtful script and naturalistic performances in the Donmar's close setting.
